gateway.text:
The immune system does not recognize “cancer” with one universal detector. Different immune cells use different clues and rules.

For conventional T cells, a cancer cell—or another cell that has taken up tumor material—can display a short protein fragment on a surface molecule called **HLA** (human leukocyte antigen). A **T-cell receptor (TCR)** checks the combined HLA–fragment feature. If the match is suitable, and the required activation signals are present, the T cell may become able to attack. This is a chain of steps: a DNA change must affect a protein, a fragment must be produced and displayed, and a T cell must recognize it [Follow the route to immune recognition](/education/guides/start-here/02-follow-immune-recognition/#think-of-a-team-with-different-jobs).

Other immune systems work differently. Antibodies recognize accessible molecular shapes, while natural killer cells weigh activating and inhibitory signals. Even finding T cells in a tumor does not prove they recognize cancer or can kill it [The map](/education/guides/how-the-immune-system-fights-cancer/index/#the-map).

Would you like to explore **T-cell recognition**, **antibodies**, or **how tumors evade recognition** next?
